title: Three hundred (Judges 7)
hook: the army is cut to three hundred so no one thinks numbers won

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon's fleece, wet and then dry, a doubter's sign given twice. Your line was doubt is allowed. Today, the army he gathered starts to shrink.

Thirty-two thousand men camp by the spring of Harod, with Midian spread out in the valley below. For a man who asked for sign after sign, it should be a comfort. Then the Lord speaks to Gideon, and it's the last thing a nervous general wants to hear. Not: you need more. The opposite. The people that are with thee are too many.
screen: `THIRTY-TWO THOUSAND BY THE SPRING.` → `NOT TOO FEW.` → `TOO MANY.`

segments.voice: The reason is given straight out: "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me." If a big army wins, everyone credits the big army. So the cutting starts. Whoever is fearful and trembling may go home. Twenty-two thousand leave; ten thousand stay. Still too many. Gideon brings them down to the water, and the Lord sorts them by how they drink. Three hundred bring the water up in their hands and lap it. The rest kneel down to drink, and go home. The text never says why lapping was the test; the point seems to be the cut, not the method. Then a tender detail. That night God tells Gideon to attack, and adds: if you're afraid, take your servant Purah and go listen at the edge of the camp first. Even now, the fear is planned for. Gideon overhears a soldier telling a dream: a loaf of barley bread tumbles into the camp and flattens a tent. The battle itself is strange. The three hundred carry shofars, and torches hidden inside empty jars. They surround the camp, smash the jars, blow, and shout: "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon." Then they stand, each man in his place, and the camp panics and flees. In the story, three hundred were enough, because the numbers were never what won.
screen: `TOO MANY, OR THEY'LL CREDIT THEMSELVES.` · `THE AFRAID GO HOME.` · `THREE HUNDRED WHO LAPPED.` · `JARS, TORCHES, SHOFARS: STAND IN PLACE.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open and empty in your lap, and breathe. Picture one ordinary task done with less than you think you need, fewer words, one dish instead of three, and notice that it's enough. If you pray, let the shout of the three hundred remind you who gets the credit.
Three hundred. The ones left after the fearful went home and the rest were sorted at the water, so no one could say their own hand saved them.
Your line: fewer is enough. The jars broke, and the light got out. Day seven hundred nineteen, done.

howItsDone: Jews read Gideon's three hundred as part of studying Judges, and teachers often point to the stated reason for the cut: so that Israel would not say its own hand had saved it.

chat.says: Why would God shrink Gideon's army? Wouldn't more soldiers make winning easier?
options: So no one could say their own hand saved them; the numbers were never what won.
The others deserted on their own, and God had to make do with who was left.
Gideon couldn't feed so many men in the valley, so he sent most of them home.
chat.meaning: The text gives the reason: lest Israel say, mine own hand hath saved me. The army is cut down on purpose.

Harod.meaning: the spring where Gideon's army camped

Purah.meaning: Gideon's servant, who went with him to listen at the camp

Midian.meaning: the people camped in the valley below

shofars.meaning: rams' horns, blown by the three hundred

notes: Audit: last line of the teach framed as the story's view ('In the story, ...') rather than the narrator's own claim about who won the battle.
Numbers (thirty-two thousand, twenty-two thousand, ten thousand, three hundred) are all stated in Judges 7:3 and 7:6.
Judges 7:2 and 7:20 quoted from the KJV; JPS 1917 renders 7:20 differently ('The sword for the LORD and for Gideon!' as remembered), so KJV is used for certainty. A Keeper may prefer JPS.
'The people that are with thee are too many' (7:2) is in the hook unquoted; it matches the KJV.
'The rest kneel down' paraphrases 7:6 (all the rest of the people bowed down upon their knees).
The fork's 'answer' reports what the text records, not a moral test.
